draft.briefing: Hey, you're in Reis Magos! Right across the Mandovi from Panjim, this village is named for the Three Wise Men of the Bible, and its church was the first in Bardez.
draft.hungryLine: For a proper meal, cross over to Panjim, where restaurants line the busy 18th June Road.

moodReplies.show-me-around: Reis Magos Fort is a 1 min walk, the Reis Magos Church is 2 min away and the lighthouse is about 8 min.
moodReplies.somewhere-to-chill: Stand by the fort and look across the Mandovi to Panjim, the capital, on the other bank.
moodReplies.surprise-me: The Mandovi in front of you was once called the Rio de Goa, and it's still described as the lifeline of the state.

tips.title: Dress modestly at the church.
tips.body: Reis Magos Church is a working church, so cover up when you go in.

tips.title: Add the Houses of Goa Museum.
tips.body: Architect Gerard da Cunha's museum at Salvador-do-Mundo in Bardez shows how eastern and western building styles blended, and opens Tuesday to Sunday.

story.title: Rio de Goa
story.body: The Mandovi, once known as the Rio de Goa, has always been Goa's lifeline. Panaji and Old Goa both sit on its other bank.

story.title: Fort and church
story.body: The village carries the Portuguese name for the Three Wise Men. It became famous for the Reis Magos Church, the first in Bardez, and the Reis Magos Fort.

story.title: Across the river
story.body: On 18 June 1946, Ram Manohar Lohia called a meeting in Panjim to end Portuguese rule. A Panjim street is still named 18th June Road after that day.

story.title: Facing the capital
story.body: Reis Magos sits on the northern bank of the Mandovi in Bardez, looking straight across at the state capital.
